title: Iowa launches nation's first Workforce Pell Grant program for EMT students - NewsBreak
text:
By Katie Kaplan ,
1 days ago
FORT DODGE, Iowa (WHO) — On Tuesday, Gov. Kim Reynolds announced that Iowa will be the first state in the nation to participate in a new federal Workforce Pell Grant program aimed at expanding access to career and technical education.
The announcement came at Iowa Central Community College, where Reynolds was joined by U.S. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon and Acting U.S. Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling.
The program is designed to help address workforce shortages by providing up to $7,500 in financial assistance for select short-term training programs, between 8 and 15-weeks long.
“It isn’t a prestigious diploma that makes the difference, but the rigorous training, precision, coordination and practice skill that you each bring to the job,” said McMahon.
Story continues below
According to Reynolds, Iowa is expected to have more than 500 Emergency Medical Technician (EMT) job openings over the next five years. Recruiting for those positions can be especially challenging in rural areas because of the cost of training and the time required to become certified, she said.
Students enrolled in Iowa Central Community College’s 14-week EMT program will be the first in the country to receive funding through the Workforce Pell Grant partnership.
“Our purpose at Iowa Central is simple: to help students earn a degree or credential as quickly as possible, with as little debt as possible, so they can build a better life, said ICCC president Dr. Jesse Ulrich.
Reynolds said the initiative will eventually expand to nine programs across four of Iowa’s community colleges.
“By focusing programs on Iowa’s most critical labor needs, like healthcare, manufacturing, skilled trades and IT we’re actively and intentionally building our talent pipeline for the future,” she said.
The Workforce Pell Grant program supports short-term workforce training in high-demand fields, giving students another pathway into careers that do not require a traditional four-year degree.
“Across the board, we’re seeing students who before didn’t have the path, becoming now electricians, carpenters, plumbers- what the American economy needs,” said Sonderling.
Unlike traditional Pell Grants, the Workforce Pell Grant pilot may also be available to people who already hold a college degree but are seeking additional training because they are struggling to make ends meet.
Iowa was the first state to submit an application for the pilot program, making it the first to be selected. The program will operate for one year before students become fully eligible for Workforce Pell Grant funding.
